2 trades, 2 wins today - entries have ceased to be my issue for some weeks and months now.

My biggest problem remains, not running my trades properly. I enter off some M15/M30 setup, and then stare at the thing on M1 and exit off some stupid small level after a single pin.

Having a micro account doesn't help with this - ideally I would take some off, take a bit more off, let the rest run - but when you're only trading at 0.01 and 0.02, your options are extremely limited.

It's just fear - fear of watching the open profit on the trade go all the way back to zero, or even stop me out for a loss.

But until I get this under control, I will be putting massive pressure on myself to win a very high % of my entries.

The only time I run trades well is when they surge away from entry, and there is little doubt that you've got a decent move on your hands. Those that accumulate for a while, before sort of slithering away, kill me, even though many times they end up being big moves.

Thoughts on how to be more zen whilst running trades which have gone into good profit, but you believe can go a lot further, are welcome

Another benefit to trading a large number of instruments - correlations. Think CADJPY is about to go long? Quickly check UCAD - is it at a level it could go short from? Great, take the trade. Is it in the middle of a PAZ? Probably better wait.

As discussed previously, individual instruments do not exist in a vacuum. The Fx market is driven by money flowing from one set of currencies into others. It is no coincidence that when an entire currency is about to make a turn, it's major and minors are usually all at significant levels at the same time. In this way we can also usually get a good guess at which directions large news announcements are going to go - 5-10 mins out from GBP news for example, go check the big picture on all GBP crosses, see if they are sat at important levels, or have just turned from important levels 30 mins ago etc.

If you're looking at a setup on an individual minor crosspair, and none of the other crosses for this currency are reflecting the same PA or are at good levels, then you should probably wait.

I wrote this indi a little while back to help me out with this - it enables me to quickly look at all crosses for a given currency at once, without needing the chart open. It inverts those crosses that need inverting, so that they're all the correct way up with respect to the currency being viewed.

Thanks for that. I think a lot of the issue currently is *needing* to make money, because I'm broke. If I was sat here, with a ton of cash in the bank already, it would be much easier to just let things run. But it's a bit of a catch22 currently.

I've lost count of the number of trades I closed for 10 pips at FTA that went on to make 100 or 200+ pips.

Thinking about it, one of the reasons I find it hard to hold a trade, is that "engulfs" seem to be so much less reliable as time is moving forwards.

I'm always much more comfortable hitting FTB to a strong level, and running it as far as the first decent surge will allow.

Think about how many times price reacts to a valid level, appears to engulf, but then just turns around and keeps going the way it was, and breaks the level that originally held.

Take this example from AJ today:

My strengths lie in finding areas I know there is an extremely high chance of price reacting to FTB. My weakness is then in determining how far I can realistically hold the trade, unless price makes a massive surge away from entry and makes it easy for me.

Now I am sounding like a heretic, but does not engulfs have an element of "after the fact" thinking? - what does an engulf show but one side being stronger than another -does it have to be to the pip or a law? In my view it is just a way to observe the current sentiment, just as higher highs, higher lows, price moving higher, price moving lower will do the same.

Certainly, it's just a single piece of information out of many that must be taken into consideration. But the engulf is one of our main weapons of determining how far a move can potentially go.

The theory being that there are key price levels in the market, as defined by important FTRs (amongst other things), that contain many orders, which are defended. Once those orders are removed, price is therefore free to travel to the next important cluster, or the edge of the next PAZ.

The confusion comes when you realise there are many more types of level price can make a valid bounce from, not just FTRs. In this way, an important FTR can appear to be engulfed, but in fact price has made a valid turn from another type of level. The more that price FOs, the more confusing this picture becomes, and the harder it is to know exactly how far we can hold a trade.

Higher highs and lower lows are by themselves somewhat meaningless unless viewed in the context of FTRs/PAZ. A higher high that was rejected from MPL of an important bearish FTR is in fact a reversal signal, not a continuation signal for instance.

Ideally, when we enter a trade, we want to see price engulf the nearest important level in our favour. This is then our cue to try and hold the trade further. The harder it is to define a valid engulf however, the harder it is to have confidence to understand where price may be headed next.

Personally, all analysis begins from FTRs, from weekly downwards.

I then fit DPs on SR etc into the context of these FTRs. If the structure of the FTR appears to support it, I will attempt a trade from near MPL, otherwise I start looking for seemingly unimportant DPs on S/D levels that price can FO into or react from - but it's always in the context of important higher scale FTRs - these are our best roadmap of what price wants to do. We then fit the IT tricks in and around these.

Example - GJ short I took today i.imgur.com/MyECRTi.png

After a while, it's just the same old tricks, over and over again. The key is to learn to recognise: - which levels are likely to get ignored/faked, and where they are going to fake into - which important FTRs are good to trade from the near the edge without them breaking

I prefer the first scenario personally, because then I am either trading a reversal from genuine FO, or I am trading the RT cycle after an eng of an important level which can be large sometimes. A valid reaction to a valid levels happens far less often than the combined amount of times a FO or eng + RT happens.

The second scenario is totally valid however, and works well a lot of the time. The key to recognising which FTR edges are more likely to work is to recognise the smaller scale structure near the edge, and where it is located in relation to the next significant orders. This comes largely from experience, but generally you want to see something on smaller scale that can be faked, and something for it to fake into. Remember the ITs can't generate much LQ from turning price at a massively obvious level - if you can see if that obviously, so can the rest of the world.
UCAD - same tricks, different day. Could have run this further, I intended to monitor PA as price approached TG, but all sorts of GBP craziness was going off, and I was distracted.

Beautiful level here on GA, ticked all the right boxes - see if you can see why.

It can go up a lot more, but I only had 0.01, so closed out at QM level.

NU coming out of awesome daily level, added at the QM - this one could run for a long way, but 0.01 woes again, and I won't lie, the stress of letting the thing run for hours just kills me. It's 6pm and I want to just relax without worrying over the possibility of this trade coming back to zero on me.

I don't know if I'll ever get used to it - I think I am getting better gradually, but I really just prefer to be in and out of the market in a short space of time with high R - it's easily doable to catch a 10-20R move which is done in an hour or two.

I imagine the ability to let trades run for days comes from a few things: - much experience - having enough money in your bank so that you don't have to worry about making a lot quickly like I do! - having a big enough account size to take profit out of the trade once or twice, and let the rest run - trading at 0.01 does not facilitate this

One of the biggest breakthroughs in my trading came recently when I started trying to "think like the ITs". When considering the trade of any level, I now first ask myself - how much LQ can the ITs generate at this level?

A lot of traders are a lot more S/D savvy than they used to be. A valid turn from an obvious valid level means the ITs aren't going to get too many of their orders filled for big positions.

Instead, when considering a level, it's always a good idea to look nearby, and see if there is a better level that price was turned just before, such as this example here in the PA that is developing from the move up on GN. No guarantees this will work here - but the presence of that swing low "hovering" above the QM gives a great low risk/high RR opportunity upon return.

Always be suspicious of the "too obvious" FTR floating just above a really nice DP on a QM or SR...

Some thoughts on FTRs/FLs.

The usual disclaimer applies - this is a grossly simplified model of price movement, and in the real market, price movement is often much more nuanced.

However, as a building block of theory, it's useful to consider. When we are dealing with high scale levels such as daily or weekly, then these "inner chain" FLs can produce pretty sizable bounces, more than enough to get a great medium-term trade from.

This is a bit too "trying to know 3 steps ahead what the market is going to do" for my tastes - I just like to mark zones, study approach, take into account what we're coming off, and then decide to take the trade or not. Trying to predict much more than the next single likely move and overall direction on any given scale is an exercise in pain in my experience.

Been a bit "rabbit in the headlights" today. Passed on taking many trades at levels because I thought they were going to break, and then they didn't. Took a couple of heavy scalps early on this morning, but nothing to show other than that. No losses though. A few pairs are on big trends - these are the worst type of trading conditions for me, since I naturally favour fading. Range conditions suit me a lot better.

I'm a bit risk averse still perhaps, I like a setup to "smack me in the face" in terms of levels and PA before I'll take it - I don't think it fits my personality well to be a shotgun type trader. As I gain more experience, I will no doubt see more "smack in the face" setups which weren't apparent as such before.
